title: The Running Tab Between You and the Business That Nobody Reconciles
linkedin:
Every owner-led business we look at has one of these: a loan account between the owner and the business that nobody set out to create.

It starts small. A tight month, the owner covers payroll from a personal account. A good month, the business absorbs a personal cost. Nobody calls it a loan. It just felt like the sensible thing to do at the time.

Years pass and the balance is real money, moving in both directions, with no interest rate, no repayment terms, and no one who actually owns the decision about what happens to it.

It sits quietly on the balance sheet until someone outside the business has to make sense of it. A bank assessing serviceability for a new facility. A buyer's advisor during due diligence. The ATO, if the balance runs too long without documented terms.

None of this means the arrangement was wrong. Owners support their businesses through tight months constantly, and the reverse happens just as often. The problem is not that the money moved. It is that it was never converted into something with terms.

The fix is smaller than it sounds. An agreed interest rate, a repayment ceiling, a documented resolution. That is usually a half day conversation, not a project, once someone actually looks.

Quick one for business owners: do you actually know, right now, what the running balance is between you and your business?

Not the wages, not the dividends, the informal stuff. The month you covered a supplier payment from your own account. The time the business picked up something personal. It adds up over the years into a real number that nobody ever set terms for.

It is not a problem until a bank, a buyer, or the ATO asks you to explain it, and then it very much is.

Worth a five minute check this week. Do you know what that number is at the moment?

A pattern we see constantly across Brisbane and Queensland SMEs: an informal loan account between the owner and the business that has been building for years without anyone deciding it should.

It usually starts small. A tight month where the owner covers a supplier payment personally. A good month where the business absorbs a personal cost. None of it is planned, and none of it is a problem in itself. Owners support their businesses through cash gaps constantly, and the reverse happens just as often.

The issue shows up later, when someone outside the business needs to make sense of the balance. A bank assessing lending capacity. A buyer working through due diligence before a sale. Or the ATO, if the balance has run for a long time without documented terms.

The fix is usually straightforward once someone looks properly: an agreed interest rate, a repayment ceiling, and a short resolution that records why the arrangement exists. For most businesses, this is a half day conversation rather than a drawn out project.

If you are not sure what your own running balance actually looks like, this is a good week to find out.
